email.subject: {{first_name}}, the terms of your e-banking are changing

body.v: The terms of your e-banking agreement have been updated. Please sign in to accept them by the end of the week.
Without your acceptance, your access may be limited.

hotspots.explain: swissa1pbank.example: the digit 1 has taken the place of the letter l. This is not swissalpbank.example.
"by the end of the week": the sender sets the deadline, not you.
"your access may be limited": a threat vague enough to worry you and precise enough to make you act.
The sign-in page is on the lookalike domain. Any login details you typed there would be copied.

who.prompt: Who is really writing to you? Read the address, not just the name.
who.answer: Someone borrowing the bank's name. The address has a digit 1 instead of the letter l: swissa1pbank.example is not swissalpbank.example. The eye easily skips a character; a password manager compares the address character by character.
choices: SwissAlpBank, since it knows your first name
Your personal adviser at the bank

emotion.prompt: Which feeling is this email pressing on?
emotion.answer: Fear and haste: you could lose access if you do not act before the end of the week.
choices: Curiosity about a prize to be won
Fear of losing access, with a deadline
None, it is just a formality

ask.prompt: What does it actually want you to do?
ask.answer: Sign in to "accept" the new terms. Your login details would go to the sender.
choices: Open the agreement in the attachment

verify.prompt: How can you check through a channel you control?
verify.answer: Go through the SwissAlpBank login saved in your password manager. It only offers that login on the site whose address matches exactly: if it offers nothing, that is your warning sign. You can also open the bank's app yourself.
choices: Click the link and check the page looks normal
Use the login saved in your manager, or the app
Type the password by hand if the manager offers nothing

actions.label: Open the bank from the login saved in your password manager, or through the app
actions.consequence: Nothing to accept. And on the page from the email, the manager would not have offered your login.

actions.label: Click the link and enter your password
actions.consequence: The page looks normal, but your login details go straight to the scammer.

actions.label: The manager offers nothing, so type the password by hand
actions.consequence: It stayed silent because the address was wrong. That was your best warning, and you overrode it.

actions.label: Report it as phishing and delete it
actions.consequence: Your login details never left your hands.

attacker_reveal: Your eyes corrected it for you: one digit slipped in for a letter, and you still read the bank's name. Your password manager compares character by character. When it stays silent, believe it over your eyes.
